title: Visual directions for Nocturne
context: Nocturne is an independent cinema with three auditoriums. Staff plan the day's programming on a desktop dashboard, the audience buys seats on their phone and the lobby TV shows tonight's films. Made-up product for the skill's example.
fixed: Same three screens and the same data in every direction
Status is always a dot or icon plus text
Contrast AA in light and dark
how_to_read: Three directions, three screens: the programming dashboard, the seat picker on a phone and the lobby TV. Start with the lobby from across the room, then check how fast you find the sold-out session on the dashboard.
fictional_data: Nocturne, its auditoriums, occupancy, prices and «Salt Hours» (and its director) are made up. The classic films are public domain; showtimes are invented. Photos from Unsplash.

directions.name: Marquee
directions.tagline: The lights go down, the picture takes over.
directions.idea: A late-night film programme: warm darkness, a serif that feels printed, and the photograph always leading. Gold is used once per screen, like the bulbs on a marquee.
directions.signature: Film titles set large in Fraunces over a full-bleed still that fades into the room.

axes.imagery: Large photos that lead each screen

pros: Feels like a cinema, not a spreadsheet
The lobby board reads as part of the building
Dark mode is the natural state for a screening room
cons: Fewer rows per screen on the dashboard
Depends on good photography for every film

dashboard: The selected film opens with its still at full width; the timeline stays quiet until you pick a session.
Gold marks only the selected session and the primary action.
mobile: The film still sits behind the header, so buying a seat still feels like going to the movies.
Selected seats are gold; taken seats simply recede.
lobby: Half the board is the room itself; titles in Fraunces read like a printed programme from across the lobby.

directions.name: Ticket Stub
directions.idea: The paper side of cinema: cream stock, black ink, times printed in monospace and a perforated edge where you tear. Everything fits, nothing decorates.
directions.signature: Perforated edges and monospace times, as if every session were a printed stub.
directions.references: Linear, Teenage Engineering, cinema ticket stock

axes.typography: Hanken Grotesk + IBM Plex Mono for times

pros: Most sessions per screen: the whole day fits without scrolling
Times in monospace line up and scan fast
Cheap to build: no photography needed
cons: Less emotional on the public screens
Paper texture can look dated if overused

dashboard: All ten sessions and the timeline fit on one screen; the film detail is a stub with a perforated edge.
Blue ink appears only on the selected session and the primary button.
mobile: The ticket is the screen: a tear line separates the seat map from the stub you keep.
lobby: A printed board: each session is a stub, times in monospace, the screen number in a box.

directions.name: Projector
directions.tagline: Big type, hard light, no guessing.
directions.idea: Signage first: a cold, high-contrast system of solid blocks and one electric blue, built to be read from the back of the lobby and reused on the dashboard.
directions.signature: Screen numbers as solid square blocks, and heavy Archivo set tight at signage size.
pros: Best legibility at distance: the lobby board works from 10 m
Screen numbers become wayfinding the building can reuse
Very clear status at a glance
cons: Blocks can feel loud on a staff tool used all day

dashboard: The black rail and blue blocks make the tool feel like the building's signage.
Timeline sessions are solid blocks; the selected one turns blue.
mobile: Seat map with square seats and a heavy total; the pay button is the only blue on screen besides your seats.
lobby: Black board, screen numbers as big blue squares, times at 64 px: readable from the door.

comparison.note: Dots from 1 to 5, judged by eye with the same data in all three.

mix_rule: Mix one direction's composition with another's type or density; never two accent colors on the same screen.

mixes.title: Ticket Stub for staff, Marquee for the audience
mixes.text: The dense paper dashboard for the people who program, with Marquee's photos and serif on the phone and in the lobby. Share the gold accent so the brand stays one.

mixes.title: Marquee with Projector's screen blocks
mixes.text: Keep Marquee's warmth and photography, but borrow the solid screen-number squares as wayfinding.

mixes.title: Ticket Stub seat map in Marquee colors
mixes.text: The tear line and monospace seat labels from Ticket Stub, on Marquee's dark warm palette for evening buyers.

mixes.title: Projector dashboard with Marquee's detail panel
mixes.text: Projector's hard timeline blocks for scanning, with Marquee's photo-led film panel on the right.

recommendation.title: Marquee, with Ticket Stub density on the dashboard
recommendation.summary: Marquee is the one that feels like Nocturne: the photograph and the serif carry the brand onto the phone and the lobby, and the dark base suits a cinema. Tighten the dashboard with Ticket Stub's row height.
why: The audience-facing screens (phone and lobby) are where the brand is felt, and Marquee wins both.
The sold-out session is still found in one glance: gold selection, rose status with text.
Passes AA in light and dark; dark is the default after 18:00.
recommendation.alternative: if the lobby TV is the priority and there is no budget for film stills, Projector is the safer choice.
steps: Paste marquee/tokens.css into the global stylesheet.
Copy the signature from directions/marquee.css (photo-led detail panel and title treatment).
Set --row-h to 36px on the dashboard only.
Rebuild the three screens with the project's components.
recommendation.question: Which one do you pick, or shall we mix? (recommended: Marquee)
